open_points.subject: A20 Python dependency identity
open_points.question: What concrete Python artifact is named by the required digest and compared when the Python digest differs?
options: Digest the exact Python distribution archive used to build or install the runtime.
Digest the installed interpreter executable or a canonical runtime tree.
Treat Python as part of the base image and define its separate digest as the digest of a specified image constituent.
open_points.default_guess: Digest the exact Python distribution archive from which the runtime is installed.

witness.initial: A release names Python 3.14.0 and a base-image digest; the host has a Python interpreter whose executable bytes match one build but whose source or distribution archive differs.
events: The release process records a digest for Python 3.14.0.
The installer compares the available Python runtime with that digest.
One implementation hashes the distribution archive; another hashes the installed interpreter executable.
outcomes: The archive-hashing installer refuses the installation and no instance starts.
The executable-hashing installer accepts the installation and starts the instance.
witness.observer: The owner installing the release sees whether the instance starts.

open_points.subject: A20 release identity
open_points.text: A dependency changes only by a new release, verified as any release.
open_points.question: What makes a release the same release, and may a release identifier or version be rebound to different dependency contents?
options: A release identity is immutable and content-addressed; different dependency contents necessarily have a different release identity.
A release has an immutable unique version or build identifier that may never be rebound.
A reused public version is allowed, but each publication receives a distinct internal release identity.
open_points.default_guess: Make every release identity immutable and content-addressed; reject rebinding of any published release identifier.

witness.initial: Release identifier 1.0 names dependency list L1 and has already been installed once.
events: A publisher later associates identifier 1.0 with dependency list L2.
The owner installs what is presented as release 1.0 again.
One implementation treats the identifier as the release identity; another treats the new publication or contents as a new release.
outcomes: The first implementation refuses the change because the same release must give L1.
The second implementation accepts L2 as a new release despite reuse of the visible identifier.
witness.observer: The owner and the running instance see different installed dependency lists for the visible release identifier 1.0.

open_points.subject: A20 Required tests item 2
open_points.text: A release whose list misses a package the instance would import, or names a package, the Python version or the base image without an exact version or a digest, is not made.
open_points.question: Must the release-process tests also show that a release is not made when the list entirely omits the Python dependency or entirely omits the base image?
options: Add separate missing-Python and missing-base-image cases to Required test 2.
State that the release representation makes those omissions impossible and require a check that demonstrates that structural guarantee.
Weaken the normative completeness rule so only missing packages are a required refusal.
open_points.default_guess: Add explicit missing-Python and missing-base-image refusal cases to Required test 2.

witness.initial: A candidate release lists every Python package and the base image with complete identities but contains no Python entry.
events: The release process validates the candidate.
One test suite applies the normative completeness rule to every dependency kind.
Another test suite implements only the omission case expressly named in Required test 2: a missing package.
outcomes: The first suite demonstrates that the candidate release is not made.
The second suite can pass without ever showing the required refusal for an omitted Python entry; the analogous omission of the base image is also unshown.
witness.observer: The release reviewer sees different claimed test coverage for the same completeness guarantee.

open_points.subject: A20 release dependency representation
open_points.text: names a package, the Python version or the base image without an exact version or a digest
open_points.question: How will the release and deployment artifacts represent the separate exact-version and digest identities for packages, Python and the base image?
options: Store distinct canonical name, exact-version and digest fields for every dependency kind.
Use kind-specific immutable references, with deployment tooling deterministically decomposing each reference into its version and digest.
Generate a lock or provenance document whose typed entries carry the required identities and make that document the installer's input.
consequences: Distinct fields make completeness checks direct but require a common schema across unlike dependency kinds.
Kind-specific references fit native package and OCI conventions but require precise normalization rules.
A generated lock or provenance document centralizes verification but makes its schema and generation step part of the deployment interface.
open_points.requirement:
A release names every dependency it runs with, at an exact version, with
   its digest: every Python package, direct or transitive, by the digest of
   its distribution file; the Python version; and the base image of VM
   Platform's Registry environment by its digest, which fixes the system
   libraries and the store's engine.
open_points.default_guess: Use a typed generated lock document with explicit name, exact-version and digest fields for each dependency entry.
